intro: Casino cage workers handle large sums, follow strict procedures and serve customers, skills that casino management rewards. The closest of the 25 careers below is gambling and sports book writing, with a 92% match, while gambling services supervisors are 91% matched and earn a BLS May 2025 median of $63,820, or 70% more.
why_it_works: Working the cage means counting and tracking cash precisely, verifying transactions and staying calm with impatient customers. O*NET rates social perceptiveness, time management and service orientation at 3 out of 5 for this job. Casino supervision, postal and cashier jobs use the same skills. Almost every match needs no extra schooling. The gaps are problem solving and managing people.
tips: Gambling Managers earn $93,220, which is 148% more, and many start in the cage.
Postal Service Clerks earn $62,130, or 65% more, and handle cash and public service.
Ask to train new cage staff; supervising people is your main skill gap.

faq.q: What jobs can former casino cage workers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are gambling and sports book writers (92%), gambling services supervisors (91%) and gambling change persons and booth cashiers (90%), based on O*NET 31.0. Cashiers are 88% matched but earn $32,880, which is 13% less than the $37,580 cage worker median.

faq.q: Which careers for casino cage workers pay more?
faq.a: 16 of the 25 matches pay more. Gambling Managers earn $93,220 (148% more), gambling services supervisors $63,820 (70% more) and Postal Service Clerks $62,130 (65% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Casino promotions usually come from experienced floor staff.

faq.q: Do cage workers need more education to switch?
faq.a: Rarely. 24 of the 25 matches need no more education than gambling cage workers already have, including 9 of the top 10. In the closest match, 87% of workers have a high school diploma or the equivalent, so your cash handling record and gaming license history usually matter more than formal schooling.

faq.q: What skills should cage workers learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are complex problem solving, managing people, managing materials and systems analysis. Judgment already rates 2.88 out of 5 for this job in O*NET, so supervising a shift is the main step toward casino management.
